subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Solve the equation x⁴ − 4x² + 8x + 35 = 0, given that 2 + i√3 is a root of the equation.

mark_split.label: The conjugate 2 − i√3 is also a root
Solve x² + 4x + 5 = 0 and list all four roots

Correction to the book, recorded not silently fixed: p.26 prints 'the equation with roots 2 + √3, 2 − √3 is x² − (sum of roots)x + product = 0' — the i is dropped in that one line; the roots are 2 ± i√3 and the book's own sum (4), product (7) and factor x² − 4x + 7 are the correct ones for 2 ± i√3 (for 2 ± √3 the product would be 1). The book divides by the two-row synthetic method with 4 and −7; the card shows the same division long-hand. Truth check: (x² − 4x + 7)(x² + 4x + 5) expands to x⁴ − 4x² + 8x + 35; the four roots add to 0 (no x³ term) and multiply to 7 · 5 = 35, the constant term. recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — what the given root tells you about a second root, how the pair becomes a factor, and how you find the other two roots.
insider_note: The product of the conjugate pair is 4 + 3 = 7, not 4 − 3 = 1; the i² = −1 is where this question is most often lost.

steps.label: Conjugate root
steps.margin_note: First mark. The coefficients are real, so complex roots come in conjugate pairs: 2 − i√3 is a root too. Say why — the word 'real coefficients' is what earns the mark.
lines: The coefficients are real, so complex roots
2 + i√3 is a root ⇒ 2 − i√3 is also a root.

recall.must_convey: That because the coefficients are real, the conjugate 2 − i√3 is also a root.
accept: the coefficients are real so the conjugate two minus i root three is also a root
complex roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs so two minus i root three is a root
the conjugate is also a root because the equation has real coefficients
coefficients real kabatti conjugate two minus i root three kuda root avutundi
take the conjugate as the second root

steps.why: A polynomial with real coefficients cannot have a single non-real root: if z is a root, so is its conjugate z̄, because conjugation respects sums and products and leaves real coefficients unchanged. That doubles the given information with no extra work.
common_mistakes: Not stating that the coefficients are real, which is the reason the conjugate is a root.
Writing the conjugate as −2 − i√3 (only the sign of the imaginary part changes).

steps.label: Quadratic factor
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The pair's sum is 4 and product is 4 − 3i² = 7 (i² = −1, so −3i² = +3). The quadratic with these roots, x² − 4x + 7, divides f(x).
lines: Sum of the pair = (2 + i√3) + (2 − i√3) = 4

recall.must_convey: That the sum (4) and product (7) of the conjugate pair give the quadratic factor x² − 4x + 7.
accept: sum of the pair is four and product is seven so x squared minus four x plus seven is a factor
the two conjugate roots give the quadratic factor x squared minus four x plus seven
form x squared minus sum x plus product from the pair
pair sum four product seven, kabatti x square minus four x plus seven factor
product is four plus three because i squared is minus one
heard_as: x squared minus four x plus seven

steps.why: Two known roots α, β give the factor (x − α)(x − β) = x² − (α + β)x + αβ. Using sum and product keeps the i's out of the long division: the factor has real coefficients even though its roots do not.
common_mistakes: Writing x² + 4x + 7 (the sign of the middle term is minus the sum).
Trying to divide by (x − 2 − i√3) directly, which carries i through the whole division.

steps.label: Divide f(x)
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Divide x⁴ + 0x³ − 4x² + 8x + 35 by x² − 4x + 7. Each line: take the leading term, multiply the divisor, subtract. The remainder must be 0; the quotient is x² + 4x + 5.

recall.must_convey: That f(x) is divided by x² − 4x + 7 with zero remainder, giving the quotient x² + 4x + 5.
accept: divide f of x by x squared minus four x plus seven, remainder zero, quotient x squared plus four x plus five
long division by the quadratic factor leaves x squared plus four x plus five
the other factor is x squared plus four x plus five
x square minus four x plus seven tho divide chesthe quotient x square plus four x plus five
f of x factorises as the two quadratics
heard_as: x squared plus four x plus five

steps.why: Removing the known quadratic factor leaves a quadratic, which the formula can finish. The zero remainder is the proof that x² − 4x + 7 really is a factor — if it is not zero, step 2 was wrong.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the 0x³ term, so the columns do not line up.
A sign slip when subtracting (subtracting −4x³ adds 4x³).
Not writing the remainder 0, which is the check the examiner looks for.

steps.label: Remaining roots
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. x² + 4x + 5 = 0 has discriminant 16 − 20 = −4, so √(−4) = 2i and the roots are −2 ± i. Box all four; the sum is 4 + (−4) = 0, matching the missing x³ term.
lines: The other two roots solve x² + 4x + 5 = 0:

recall.must_convey: That x² + 4x + 5 = 0 is solved by the formula to give −2 ± i, and all four roots are listed together.
accept: solve x squared plus four x plus five equals zero, discriminant minus four, roots minus two plus or minus i, and list all four
the quotient gives minus two plus or minus i so the roots are two plus or minus i root three and minus two plus or minus i
use the quadratic formula on the quotient and write all four roots
quotient solve chesthe minus two plus or minus i, anni four roots raayali
the last pair is minus two plus or minus i
heard_as: minus two plus or minus i

steps.why: The quotient's discriminant is negative, so the last two roots are also a conjugate pair — a degree-4 real polynomial with one non-real root must have an even number of them. The sum of all four is 0, which is the coefficient of the missing x³ term.
common_mistakes: Boxing only the two new roots and leaving out the given pair.
Not checking: the four roots must add to 0 (no x³ term) and multiply to 35 (7 × 5).
